PRESCHOOL · AGE 3 · CLASS 1

Alphabet & Letter Sounds

Age 3 YearsClass Preschool 1Subjects Letters, sounds & matching

Twenty-six alphabet cards, a whole pile of familiar things to name, and printable sheets to solve at the table. This is the first preschool class on the path — built for three-year-old pacing, which means short, playful and always allowed to stop.

You do not need to teach the whole alphabet today. Start with a few letters that catch your child’s eye — the first letter of their name is the classic winner — and let the rest wait for next time.

Start Today’s Class ↓Grown-up nearby, little one on the lap or roaming — both work.

TODAY’S CLASS

How today’s class works.

Five little steps, in any order that suits you: a welcome from your teacher, the letter cards, big-and-little letters on the printed sheets, an off-screen hunt, and a warm goodbye. Stop after any step — that is a complete class, and there is never a score at the end.

  1. 1 Teacher welcome
  2. 2 Learn the letters
  3. 3 Solve the sheets
  4. 4 Take it off screen
  5. 5 Class complete
TEACHER WELCOME

“Hello, my friend — and hello to you, grown-up helper! Today we are playing with letters. Start with a few that catch your child’s eye; you can always come back for more.”

— Your Kiddo School teacher

SOLVE THE SHEETS — ON PAPER OR ON SCREEN

Solve the alphabet sheets together.

The twenty-six letter cards print two to a page, straight from your browser. Printed, cut and named, they are the class’s real worksheets — and on screen, every card page can be drawn on directly.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Open the printable cards and print all twenty-six, two to a page. Cut them out together, saying each letter’s name as it is cut.

  2. 02

    Say letter, then sound

    Hold up a card and say both in one breath — “B, and it says buh”. Then let your child have the card and take a turn.

  3. 03

    Sort big and little

    Lay the cards out and find each big letter’s little partner. Same letter, different size — matching them is real letter work.

  4. 04

    Trace, then color

    Pick today’s card and trace its big letter with one finger, then a crayon. On screen, the card page has a Write & Color layer that does the same job.

Open the printable cards ↗Draw on the cards on screen ↗

Every card page has a Write & Color layer: your child can draw right on the card with a finger, a stylus or the mouse, then save the finished work. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Letters that live in your house.

The alphabet sticks best away from the screen, in short playful moments. Pick one of these — two minutes is plenty — and follow your child’s lead.

Find their own letter

  • Say the first letter of your child’s name and look for it on cups, clothes and cereal boxes.
  • “That’s your letter!” is the whole game — and it never gets old.

Letter hunt on a book cover

  • Hold up a favourite picture book and ask, “Can you find a letter you know on the cover?”
  • Any letter they spot is a win — name it warmly and move on.

Playdough letters

  • Roll a long rope of playdough and bend it into the first letter of your child’s name — or today’s favourite card letter.
  • Letters you can squeeze are letters you remember.

Letters out in the world

  • On a walk or a shop trip, point out letters on signs and packaging — “Look, an S like sun!”
  • Keep it light: one or two letters per outing is exactly right.

Stay close, keep it playful and stop while it is still fun. There is nothing to finish here.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

At three, letter play is recognition play: naming, noticing and drawing — not drilling or handwriting. If your child mixes up b and d, or loves Q only for its tail, that is exactly on track. The printed sheets and the Write & Color layer keep every sound claim on the cards honest — including x, which mostly ends words rather than starting them.

TIPS FOR PARENTS

How to use this class.

Sit together for the card viewing — laps are the best seats in the house. Name the letter and say its sound in the same breath — “B, and it says buh” — then move on quickly. Letter names and letter sounds are both worth knowing, and mixing them in play keeps either one from feeling like a test.

On the printed sheets, let the finger do the tracing first and the crayon second. On screen, let your child do the drawing in the Write & Color layer — even when the letter looks wobbly; the finger teaches the eye.

Age 3 is a guide, not a deadline. If today’s class is two letters traced on a printed sheet, today’s class was a success.
